key_terms.meaning: Many optical carriers of different wavelengths share one fiber, each carrying its own channel; capacity C = N × B.
Δλ = λ²Δf/c and Δf = cΔλ/λ²; 100 GHz at 1550 nm is 0.80 nm. The comb from λ1 to λN spans (N − 1)Δf.
DWDM: 100 GHz, 50 GHz or finer on the ITU grid anchored at 193.1 THz. CWDM: 20 nm spacing, 18 channels from 1270 to 1610 nm.
Planar device: waveguides with a fixed length step between two slabs focus each wavelength on its own output.
CR = P₃/(P₃ + P₄); excess loss 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/(P₃ + P₄)) dB; insertion loss 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₃) dB; directivity 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₂) dB.
An ideal 1×N splitter or N×N star gives 10 log₁₀ N dB to each port (15.05 dB for N = 32).
Isolator: polarizer, 45° Faraday rotator, 45° polarizer; passes one way. Circulator: routes port 1 → 2 → 3 with no 3 dB split.
Periodic core index with pitch Λ; reflects the Bragg wavelength λ<sub>B</sub> = 2 n<sub>eff</sub> Λ and passes the rest.
Er³⁺-doped fiber pumped at 980 or 1480 nm; gain 20 to 40 dB over 1530 to 1565 nm, NF 4 to 6 dB.
G = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>out</sub>/P<sub>in</sub>) dB; NF = 10 log₁₀(SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub>), about 3 dB at best.
PCE = (P<sub>s,out</sub> − P<sub>s,in</sub>)/P<sub>p</sub> ≤ λ<sub>p</sub>/λ<sub>s</sub> (0.632 for a 980 nm pump).
OSNR ≈ 58 + P<sub>in</sub>(dBm) − NF − 10 log₁₀ N dB in 0.1 nm at 1550 nm.
A laser chip with anti-reflection facets; 20 to 30 dB gain, NF 6 to 9 dB, polarization dependent, fast gain causes cross-gain modulation.
n = n₀ + n₂I with n₂ ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W; γ = 2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>), about 1.3 W⁻¹km⁻¹ for A<sub>eff</sub> = 80 µm².
φ<sub>NL</sub> = γP L<sub>eff</sub>, L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − e<sup>−αL</sup>)/α; δω = −dφ<sub>NL</sub>/dT gives a red leading edge and a blue trailing edge.
N² = L<sub>D</sub>/L<sub>NL</sub> = 1 with L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂|, L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀); P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²), β₂ < 0, FWHM = 1.763 T₀.
An end-to-end optical connection that uses one wavelength on every link of its route.
1+1: sent on both paths, receiver selects; 1:1: backup may carry extra traffic; 1:N: one backup for N paths.
H1, H2 bytes in the line overhead that give where the floating payload starts, so a tributary can be added or dropped.
Drops chosen wavelengths to local equipment and adds new ones, passing all other wavelengths through unchanged.
Without converters a lightpath needs one wavelength free on every link: S = S₁ ∩ … ∩ S<sub>k</sub> must not be empty.
53 bytes: 5-byte header and 48-byte payload. AAL5 pads data and adds an 8-byte trailer to fill whole cells.

takeaways: WDM raises fiber capacity by adding wavelengths, C = N × B, not by making the electronics faster; 100 GHz spacing is 0.80 nm at 1550 nm.
Couplers, isolators, circulators and Bragg gratings set the loss and crosstalk of every WDM node; two circulators and a grating make an add-drop node.
An optical amplifier boosts all channels at once by stimulated emission; noise adds as 10 log₁₀ N over N amplifiers, and the pump-to-signal photon ratio caps the output.
The EDFA rules 1550 nm links with high gain, low noise figure and little polarization dependence; the SOA is smaller and cheaper, works near 1310 nm too, and suits gates and converters.
At high power the Kerr effect makes a pulse chirp itself through SPM; balanced against anomalous dispersion at P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²) it forms a soliton that keeps its shape.
A lightpath is one wavelength held end to end; a ring of fibers can carry a full mesh of lightpaths, and wavelength reuse cuts the wavelengths needed.
SONET/SDH packs tributaries into a 125 µs frame locked to one clock, so rates are exact multiples of 51.84 Mb/s and pointers let one channel be added or dropped cleanly.
WDM nodes combine add-drop, cross-connection and sometimes wavelength conversion; converters remove the continuity constraint at W times the switch size.
Layering keeps transmission, framing and user services independent, which is why IP, ATM and SONET/SDH can share the same fiber.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled block diagram with the governing formula, typical numeric values worked to an answer, and a clear statement of the trade-off or design choice. Most syllabi stress the WDM components, the EDFA, SONET/SDH and the optical network vocabulary.

bank.q: Define WDM. Explain how it increases the capacity of one fiber without raising the electronic bit rate, and list four advantages and two problems it brings.
outline: Definition: several modulated wavelengths on one fiber, each an independent channel
Capacity C = N × B
Mux–fiber–demux block diagram
Advantages: capacity, upgrade by adding wavelengths, transparency to bit rate and format, fewer fibers and shared amplifiers
Problems: crosstalk and nonlinearity, need for wavelength-stable lasers and filters
Closing check with a 40-channel example
answer: Definition. Wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) sends N optical carriers of different wavelengths λ1 … λN through one fiber at the same time. Each wavelength is modulated by its own data and forms an independent channel; a multiplexer combines the channels at the transmitting end and a demultiplexer separates them at the receiving end.

answer.text: Block diagram (draw it in the answer):
answer.pre:
Tx λ1 ─┐                              ┌─ Rx λ1
Tx λ2 ─┤                              ├─ Rx λ2
  …    ├─ MUX ── one fiber (+ EDFAs) ── DEMUX ─┤   …
Tx λN ─┘                              └─ Rx λN

answer: Why capacity grows. A single laser and modulator are limited to the electronic bit rate B of their drive circuits, a few to a few tens of Gb/s. The low-loss window near 1550 nm is several THz wide, far more than one channel can use. WDM puts N channels side by side in that window, so the total capacity is C = N × B while every transmitter and receiver still runs at B. Capacity is raised in the optical domain, not by faster electronics.

Spacing. Channels sit on a frequency grid; the spacing in wavelength is Δλ = λ²Δf/c. At 1550 nm a 100 GHz grid gives Δλ = (1550 × 10⁻⁹)² × 10¹¹ ÷ (3 × 10⁸) = 0.80 nm. DWDM uses 100 GHz, 50 GHz or finer spacing with temperature-controlled lasers; CWDM uses 20 nm spacing from 1270 to 1610 nm with cheap uncooled lasers.

head: Advantages
Problems
rows: Capacity N × B on one fiber
Crosstalk between neighbouring channels in filters and switches
Upgrade by lighting new wavelengths on installed fiber
Nonlinear effects (SPM, four-wave mixing) when many channels share the power
Each channel is transparent to its own bit rate and format
Lasers must hold their wavelength, and filters must track it
One EDFA amplifies all channels together; fewer fibers and regenerators
Wavelengths must be assigned across a network (continuity constraint)

answer: Where it is used: long-haul and submarine links, metro rings with add-drop nodes, and data-centre interconnects.

Closing check. A 40-channel system at 10 Gb/s per channel gives C = 40 × 10 = 400 Gb/s on one fiber; without WDM the same traffic would need 40 fibers, each with its own regenerators. The 40 channels at 100 GHz span 39 gaps = 3.9 THz = 31.2 nm, which fits inside the 35 nm erbium C-band, so one amplifier per span serves all of them.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a fused-fiber coupler and an arrayed waveguide grating. Give the parameters used to specify each.
outline: Fused biconical taper: two fibers twisted, fused and stretched; cores close enough for power to cross
Ports 1 to 4; coupling ratio, excess loss, insertion loss, directivity
AWG: input slab, array of waveguides with fixed length steps, output slab
Phase difference depends on wavelength, so each wavelength focuses on its own output
AWG parameters: channel count and spacing, insertion loss, crosstalk, passband
Comparison and a numeric check
answer: Fused-fiber coupler: construction. Two single-mode fibers are twisted together, heated until the claddings fuse, and pulled so the joint tapers down to a narrow waist. In the waist the cores are thin and close, so the guided field spreads into the cladding and reaches the other core: power moves between the fibers along the fused length.

Working. The power moves back and forth between the two cores as the light travels. Stopping the pull at the right length fixes how much leaves each output, for example 50:50 for a 3 dB coupler or 90:10 for a tap. Light enters port 1; ports 3 and 4 are the outputs and port 2 is the other input-side port.

answer.text: Coupler parameters (P<sub>in</sub> at port 1; P₂ back at port 2; P₃, P₄ out):

head: Parameter
Formula
Meaning
rows: share of the output in one arm
loss to one chosen port (split + excess)
how little returns on the input side

answer: Arrayed waveguide grating (AWG): construction. On a silica or silicon chip, an input waveguide opens into a free-propagation region (the first slab, or star coupler). The slab spreads the light into an array of many waveguides. Each waveguide is longer than its neighbour by a fixed step ΔL. The array ends in a second slab that focuses the light onto a row of output waveguides.

Working. The fixed length step ΔL gives a phase step 2πn<sub>eff</sub>ΔL/λ between neighbouring waveguides. This phase step depends on wavelength, so at the second slab the wavefront is tilted by an amount that changes with λ. Each wavelength therefore focuses on a different output waveguide: the AWG is a demultiplexer, and used backwards a multiplexer. It behaves like a diffraction grating built from waveguides.

AWG parameters: number of channels and channel spacing (for example 40 channels at 100 GHz, 0.8 nm), insertion loss, adjacent-channel crosstalk (a negative dB value, more negative is better), passband width and shape, and polarization and temperature dependence of the centre wavelengths.

Comparison. The fused coupler is cheap, simple and almost wavelength-flat for power splitting, but it does not sort wavelengths. The AWG sorts many wavelengths in one chip, at higher cost and with a few dB of insertion loss.

Closing check. A 1 × 8 splitter built from three stages of 3 dB couplers, each with 0.2 dB excess loss, gives each output a loss of 3 × 3.01 + 3 × 0.2 = 9.63 dB, so 1 mW in becomes 10<sup>−0.963</sup> = 0.109 mW at each of the 8 ports.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of an EDFA and explain the role of the pump laser, the doped fiber and the isolators. State typical gain, noise figure and pump wavelengths.
outline: Diagram: input isolator, WDM coupler with pump, Er-doped fiber, output isolator, gain-flattening filter
Three-level picture: pump to level 3, fast decay to metastable level 2, stimulated emission 2 → 1 at 1530–1565 nm
Pumps at 980 nm (low noise) and 1480 nm (more output per pump watt)
Isolators stop reflections and backward ASE
Typical gain 20–40 dB, NF 4–6 dB, C-band 1530–1565 nm
Power conversion efficiency and a numeric check

answer.pre:
signal in → [isolator] → [WDM coupler] → [Er-doped fiber, 10–30 m] → [isolator] → [gain-flattening filter] → out
                              ↑
                   [pump laser 980 or 1480 nm]

answer: Doped fiber. The core of 10 to 30 m of silica fiber holds Er³⁺ ions. These ions have a long-lived (metastable) level 2 about 0.8 eV above the ground level 1, matching photons of 1530 to 1565 nm. When more ions sit in level 2 than in level 1 (population inversion), a signal photon passing an excited ion stimulates it to fall to level 1 and emit an identical photon. Many such events along the fiber give the gain.

Pump laser. The pump creates the inversion. A 980 nm photon lifts an ion from level 1 to level 3; the ion drops within microseconds to level 2, where it stays about 10 ms, long enough to wait for a signal photon. A 1480 nm photon lifts the ion straight into the top of level 2. The WDM coupler merges the pump and the signal into the doped fiber with little loss to either. The 980 nm pump gives the more complete inversion and so the lower noise figure; the 1480 nm pump gives more signal power per pump watt.

Isolators. The doped fiber also emits spontaneously in all directions, and that light is amplified too (ASE). Reflections from connectors would send signal and ASE back through the gain and could make the amplifier oscillate like a laser. The input isolator blocks backward ASE from reaching the transmitter side; the output isolator blocks reflections from the line. The gain-flattening filter evens out the gain across the band so all WDM channels leave at about the same power.

head: Quantity
Typical value
rows: C-band 1530 to 1565 nm (L-band 1570 to 1610 nm with longer fiber)
4 to 6 dB (about 3 dB is the limit)

answer: Power limit. Each pump photon makes at most one signal photon, so the added signal power is at most (λ<sub>p</sub>/λ<sub>s</sub>)P<sub>p</sub>. The power conversion efficiency is PCE = (P<sub>s,out</sub> − P<sub>s,in</sub>)/P<sub>p</sub>, at most 980/1550 = 0.632 with a 980 nm pump.

Closing check. With 60 mW of 980 nm pump and 0.5 mW of signal in, an EDFA giving 25 mW out has G = 10 log₁₀(25/0.5) = 16.99 dB and PCE = 24.5/60 = 40.8 percent. The largest output allowed is 0.5 + 0.632 × 60 = 38.44 mW, so 25 mW is possible.

bank.q: Explain self-phase modulation. Starting from n = n₀ + n₂I, derive the intensity-dependent phase shift and the resulting frequency chirp.
outline: Kerr effect n = n₀ + n₂I, n₂ ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W
Phase φ = (2π/λ)nL; nonlinear part (2π/λ)n₂IL
I = P/A<sub>eff</sub> and loss give φ<sub>NL</sub> = γP L<sub>eff</sub>, γ = 2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>)
Chirp δω = −dφ<sub>NL</sub>/dT: red leading edge, blue trailing edge
Spectrum widens, shape unchanged at first; limit on channel power
Numeric check
answer: Kerr effect. In silica the refractive index depends on the light intensity I: n = n₀ + n₂I, where n₀ is the low-power index and n₂ ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W is the Kerr coefficient.

answer.pre:
φ = (2π/λ) n L = (2π/λ) n₀ L + (2π/λ) n₂ I L
                 linear part      nonlinear part φ<sub>NL</sub>

answer: Intensity in terms of power. The mode carries power P over an effective area A<sub>eff</sub>, so I = P/A<sub>eff</sub>. Then φ<sub>NL</sub> = (2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>)) P L = γPL, with the nonlinear coefficient γ = 2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>).

Loss. The power falls as P(z) = P e<sup>−αz</sup>, so the phase adds up over φ<sub>NL</sub> = γP ∫₀<sup>L</sup> e<sup>−αz</sup> dz = γP L<sub>eff</sub>, with L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − e<sup>−αL</sup>)/α. For a pulse, P becomes the instantaneous power P(T), so φ<sub>NL</sub>(T) = γP(T)L<sub>eff</sub>: the peak of the pulse gets the most phase.

Chirp. The instantaneous frequency is the time rate of the phase. With the field written as e<sup>i(φ − ω₀t)</sup>, the frequency shift is δω(T) = −∂φ<sub>NL</sub>/∂T = −γL<sub>eff</sub> dP/dT. On the leading edge the power rises (dP/dT > 0), so δω < 0: the front of the pulse shifts to the red. On the trailing edge dP/dT < 0, so δω > 0: the back shifts to the blue. Near the peak dP/dT = 0 and there is no shift.

Consequence. New frequencies appear on both sides, so the spectrum widens while the pulse shape is unchanged at first. Through dispersion this chirp later changes the shape: in normal dispersion it speeds the broadening; in anomalous dispersion it can cancel it (the soliton). In a WDM system it limits the power per channel.

answer.text: Closing check with the chapter’s fiber (n₂ = 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W, A<sub>eff</sub> = 80 µm², 0.2 dB/km, 80 km, 10 mW peak, T₀ = 10 ps sech pulse):

answer: So a 10 mW pulse is shifted by at most about 3.4 GHz at its edges, small against a 100 GHz grid; at 100 mW the shift grows ten times to about 34 GHz, a third of the grid spacing, which is why channel power is kept low.

bank.q: Describe the SONET/SDH frame and explain how a single low-rate channel can be added or dropped without breaking the whole signal apart.
outline: STS-1 frame 90 × 9 = 810 bytes, 125 µs, 51.84 Mb/s
Transport overhead 3 columns (section, line with H1 H2 H3), SPE 87 columns with path overhead
One master clock and byte interleaving; pointers let payloads float
ADM drops and inserts bytes in fixed positions; layers locate faults
Numeric check
answer: Synchronous principle. Every node is locked to one primary reference clock, and each tributary occupies fixed byte positions in a frame that repeats every 125 µs (8000 frames per second). Rates are therefore exact multiples: STS-n = n × 51.84 Mb/s and STM-N = N × 155.52 Mb/s.

answer.text: STS-1 frame (90 columns × 9 rows, sent row by row):
answer.pre:
| 3 columns transport overhead | 87 columns SPE                         |
| rows 1–3: section overhead   | col 1: path overhead | 86 cols payload |
| row 4: H1 H2 H3 (pointer)    |                      | (2 fixed stuff) |
| rows 4–9: line overhead      |                      |                 |

answer: SDH form. The STM-1 frame is 270 columns × 9 rows. Its first 9 columns are section overhead: regenerator section overhead in rows 1 to 3, the AU pointer in row 4 and multiplex section overhead in rows 5 to 9. The other 261 columns carry the VC-4 (path overhead plus the 149.76 Mb/s C-4).

Pointers. A tributary clock may differ slightly from the network clock. The pointer bytes (H1, H2) give the position where the payload envelope starts, and H3 is a spare byte for adjustment. If the tributary runs fast, one extra byte is carried in H3 and the pointer moves back by one; if slow, a stuff byte is inserted and the pointer moves forward. The payload floats, but its start is always known, so no data slips.

Add and drop. Because each tributary sits at known byte positions, an add-drop multiplexer reads the pointer, takes out the bytes of the channel to be dropped, writes the new channel into the same positions and passes every other byte straight through. In the older plesiochronous hierarchy, bit stuffing at every level hid each channel inside the higher rate, so the whole stream had to be demultiplexed step by step.

Layers. Section overhead is checked between regenerators, line (multiplex section) overhead between multiplexers, and path overhead end to end, so a fault is located to one part of the route. Line overhead also carries the protection-switching bytes for rings that restore traffic within 50 ms.
Closing check. 810 × 8 × 8000 = 51.84 Mb/s, and 3 × 51.84 = 155.52 Mb/s = 2430 × 8 × 8000, so one STM-1 carries exactly three STS-1 frames; transport overhead is 27/810 = 3.33 percent of the STS-1.

bank.q: A WDM link carries 40 channels spaced 100 GHz apart around 1550 nm, each at 10 Gb/s. Find the channel spacing in nm, the comb width and the occupied band in THz and nm, the total capacity, and check whether it fits in the C-band (1530 to 1565 nm).
outline: Δλ = λ²Δf/c = 0.80 nm
Comb width (N − 1)Δf = 3.9 THz = 31.23 nm
Occupied band N × Δf = 4.0 THz = 32.03 nm
Capacity 400 Gb/s
C-band in THz = 4.385 THz; 43 slots, so it fits
answer: Given: N = 40, Δf = 100 GHz = 10¹¹ Hz, λ = 1550 nm, B = 10 Gb/s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Comb width (first to last channel centre): N − 1 = 39 gaps, so 39 × 100 GHz = 3.9 THz, or 39 × 0.8008 = 31.23 nm.
Occupied band (each channel takes one 100 GHz slot): 40 × 100 GHz = 4.0 THz. In wavelength, 4.0 × 10¹² × (1550 × 10⁻⁹)² ÷ (3 × 10⁸) = 32.03 nm.
Capacity: C = N × B = 40 × 10 = 400 Gb/s in each direction. Spectral efficiency = 400 Gb/s ÷ 4.0 THz = 0.1 b/s per Hz, which shows how much room 10 Gb/s channels leave unused in each 100 GHz slot.

answer.text: The same 100 GHz spacing at other wavelengths (Δλ = λ²Δf/c):

answer: So a grid fixed in frequency is not fixed in wavelength: quote the spacing in nm only together with the wavelength at which it holds.
Fit: 4.385 THz ÷ 0.1 THz = 43.85, so the C-band holds 43 slots of 100 GHz. The 40-channel plan needs 4.0 THz, so it fits with 3 slots (0.385 THz) to spare.

Comment. Laser drift and the filter passband set how tight the spacing can be; halving the spacing to 50 GHz (0.40 nm) would fit 4.385/0.05 = 87.7, so 87 channels (870 Gb/s at 10 Gb/s each) in the same band, but needs better lasers and filters and raises crosstalk and four-wave mixing.
Closing check: the wavelength figure agrees with the frequency figure, since 35 nm ÷ 0.8008 nm = 43.7 slots, again 43 whole slots.

bank.q: An EDFA pumped with 20 mW at 980 nm gives 25 dB gain for a 1550 nm input of −20 dBm. Find the output in dBm and mW. The input SNR is 40 dB and the output SNR is 35 dB; find the noise figure. Find the power conversion efficiency and check the output against the energy-conservation limit.
outline: P<sub>out</sub>(dBm) = −20 + 25 = +5 dBm = 3.162 mW
Check: 3.16 mW is allowed
answer: Given: P<sub>in</sub> = −20 dBm, G = 25 dB, SNR<sub>in</sub> = 40 dB, SNR<sub>out</sub> = 35 dB, P<sub>p</sub> = 20 mW at λ<sub>p</sub> = 980 nm, λ<sub>s</sub> = 1550 nm.

answer.pre:
P<sub>out</sub>(dBm) = P<sub>in</sub>(dBm) + G(dB) = −20 + 25 = +5 dBm
P<sub>out</sub> = 10<sup>5/10</sup> mW = 10<sup>0.5</sup> = 3.162 mW

answer: Input in mW: P<sub>in</sub> = 10<sup>−20/10</sup> = 0.01 mW. Check: 3.162/0.01 = 316.2 = 10<sup>2.5</sup>, which is 25 dB.

answer.pre:
NF = SNR<sub>in</sub>(dB) − SNR<sub>out</sub>(dB) = 40 − 35 = 5 dB
F = 10<sup>0.5</sup> = 3.16 (the SNR falls by a factor of 3.16)

answer: Linear check: SNR<sub>in</sub> = 10<sup>4</sup> = 10 000 and SNR<sub>out</sub> = 10<sup>3.5</sup> = 3162, and 10 000/3162 = 3.16 = F. This is a typical EDFA value (4 to 6 dB) and above the 3 dB limit of a high-gain amplifier. The extra noise is amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) from excited erbium ions that decay on their own and whose photons are then amplified along the rest of the fiber.
In a chain the ASE of every amplifier adds. Five such amplifiers, each with −20 dBm in, give OSNR = 58 − 20 − 5 − 10 log₁₀ 5 = 58 − 20 − 5 − 6.99 = 26.0 dB in 0.1 nm.

Quantum conversion efficiency: QCE = PCE × λ<sub>s</sub>/λ<sub>p</sub> = 0.158 × 1.582 = 0.249, so about a quarter of the pump photons become signal photons; the rest are lost to ASE, unabsorbed pump and spontaneous decay.

Closing check: the 3.162 mW output is below the 12.66 mW limit and the 25 dB gain is below the 31.0 dB ceiling, so the figures are physically possible. Raising the input to −10 dBm (0.1 mW) would ask for 0.1 × 316.2 = 31.6 mW, above the 0.1 + 12.65 = 12.75 mW allowed, so the gain must compress to at most 10 log₁₀(12.75/0.1) = 21.1 dB: the amplifier saturates, and the 25 dB figure holds only for small inputs.

bank.q: A sech pulse with T₀ = 10 ps travels in a fiber with β₂ = −20 ps²/km and γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹. Find the dispersion length, the fundamental-soliton peak power, the nonlinear length at that power, the soliton order, the FWHM and the soliton period. Repeat L<sub>D</sub> and P₀ for T₀ = 5 ps.
outline: L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂| = 5 km
P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²) = 0.1 W
L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀) = 5 km; N² = L<sub>D</sub>/L<sub>NL</sub> = 1
FWHM = 1.763 T₀ = 17.63 ps; z₀ = (π/2)L<sub>D</sub> = 7.85 km
T₀ = 5 ps: L<sub>D</sub> = 1.25 km, P₀ = 0.4 W
Comment on power and the sign of β₂
answer: Given: T₀ = 10 ps, β₂ = −20 ps²/km (anomalous, so a bright soliton is possible), γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹.
Units of P₀: (ps²/km) ÷ (W⁻¹km⁻¹ × ps²) = W, so the formula is consistent.

Meaning. At 100 mW peak the SPM chirp exactly cancels the dispersion chirp, so the pulse keeps its 17.63 ps width at every distance. Without the nonlinearity the same pulse would be 1.54 times wider after one dispersion length (5 km) and 2.14 times wider after 10 km. The period z₀ matters for higher-order solitons (N = 2, 3, …), which return to their starting shape every 7.85 km; the fundamental soliton never changes shape.
Halving the width shortens L<sub>D</sub> four times and needs four times the peak power, because dispersion acts faster on a shorter pulse and SPM must grow to match it.

answer.text: For comparison, the same 10 ps sech pulse with the nonlinearity switched off (computed by propagating it with dispersion only):

answer: The soliton stays at 17.63 ps over the same 20 km, so at 10 Gb/s (100 ps bit slot) the dispersion-only pulse would already fill more than half its slot after 20 km, while the soliton keeps a fixed share.

Comment. A 100 mW peak is large for one channel. Soliton systems therefore use fibers with smaller |β₂| (dispersion-shifted fiber), which lowers the power needed, and amplifiers spaced well inside the soliton’s dispersion length so the average power holds the balance.
Closing check: γP₀L<sub>D</sub> = 2 × 0.1 × 5 = 1 = N², as required for the fundamental soliton.

bank.q: A 2×2 fused coupler has a 50:50 coupling ratio, 0.2 dB excess loss and 50 dB directivity. With 1 mW at port 1 and nothing at port 2, find the power at each output port in dBm and mW, the insertion loss, and the power returned at port 2.
outline: 1 mW = 0 dBm
Split 10 log₁₀ 2 = 3.01 dB plus excess 0.2 dB
Each output −3.21 dBm = 0.477 mW
Insertion loss 3.21 dB
Port 2: −50 dBm = 10 nW
Check: total out 0.955 mW gives 0.2 dB excess
answer: Given: P<sub>in</sub> = 1 mW = 10 log₁₀(1 mW/1 mW) = 0 dBm; CR = 50 percent; excess loss 0.2 dB; directivity 50 dB.

answer.text: Losses from port 1 to port 3 (and the same to port 4):
answer.pre:
split loss   = 10 log₁₀(1/0.5) = 3.01 dB
excess loss  = 0.20 dB
insertion loss = 3.01 + 0.20 = 3.21 dB

answer: Method: work in dB, subtracting the losses from the dBm input, then turn the result into mW with P(mW) = 10<sup>P(dBm)/10</sup>. Losses in dB add; powers in mW do not.
Total output: P₃ + P₄ = 0.477 + 0.477 = 0.955 mW. So 1 − 0.955 = 0.045 mW, 4.5 percent of the input, is lost inside the coupler as excess loss.
Coupling ratio check: CR = 0.477/(0.477 + 0.477) × 100 = 50 percent, as given.

Comment. A 3 dB coupler can never give more than half the power to each port, so the 3.01 dB is a design loss, not a fault; only the 0.2 dB is a loss to be reduced. The coupling ratio of a fused coupler varies with wavelength, because the power exchange along the fused length depends on λ, so a 50:50 coupler is specified for a band such as 1550 ± 40 nm. Directivity is measured by feeding port 1 and reading port 2 with the output ports terminated so that no reflection returns. High directivity matters in a two-way link: the 10 nW returned at port 2 is 50 dB below the input, small enough not to disturb a laser on that port.
Cascade: if port 3 feeds a second identical coupler, each of its outputs gets −3.21 − 3.21 = −6.42 dBm = 10<sup>−0.642</sup> = 0.228 mW. Three stages make a 1 × 8 tree with 9.63 dB to every port.
Closing check: 10 log₁₀(1/0.955) = 0.20 dB, matching the given excess loss, and 10 log₁₀(1/0.477) = 3.21 dB, matching the insertion loss.

bank.q: A four-node WDM ring (A, B, C, D) needs one bidirectional lightpath between every pair of nodes. Assign wavelengths so that the number of wavelengths is the minimum, and justify the assignment.
outline: Six lightpaths for four nodes (full mesh)
Shortest routes: four neighbour pairs use one link, two opposite pairs use two links
Load on links; lower bound from the busiest link
Any routing of the two opposite pairs shares one link, so some link carries 3
Valid 3-wavelength assignment; 2 is impossible
Continuity constraint stated
answer: Lightpaths: N(N − 1)/2 = 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6: A–B, B–C, C–D, D–A (neighbours) and A–C, B–D (opposite pairs). Without wavelength reuse this would need 6 wavelengths.

Rule used: no wavelength converters, so each lightpath keeps one wavelength on every link it uses (continuity), and two lightpaths that share a link must get different wavelengths. This is a colouring of the conflict graph.
Routing. Each neighbour pair uses its own single link. Each opposite pair has two routes of two links: A–C via B {A–B, B–C} or via D {C–D, D–A}; B–D via C {B–C, C–D} or via A {D–A, A–B}.

answer.text: Lower bound. Check every routing of the two opposite pairs:

answer: Every choice makes the two opposite-pair lightpaths share one link, and that link also carries its own neighbour lightpath. Three lightpaths on one link need three different wavelengths, so 2 wavelengths are impossible and at least 3 are needed.

answer.text: A 3-wavelength assignment (A–C via B, B–D via C):
Verify link by link that no wavelength repeats:

answer: Justification. The assignment is valid (no repeats on any link) and meets the lower bound of 3, so 3 is the minimum. Wavelength reuse saves half: 3 wavelengths instead of 6.

Method in general: route each request (shortest path first), find the busiest link (its load is a lower bound on the wavelengths), then colour the lightpaths in order of length with first fit, giving each the lowest-numbered wavelength not used on any of its links. For the 6-node ring the same method gives 15 lightpaths, 27 link uses, a busiest link of 5, and a 5-wavelength assignment, against 15 without reuse.
Closing check: link uses = 4 × 1 + 2 × 2 = 8 over 4 links, an average of 2, but the shared link carries 3, so the minimum is set by the busiest link, not by the average.

bank.q: Starting from the frame sizes, find the bit rates of STS-1, its SPE and its user payload, and of STM-1, VC-4 and C-4. Find the STM-4 and STM-16 rates, show STM-1 = STS-3, and find how many E1s one STM-1 carries and their total rate.
outline: Rate = bytes per frame × 8 × 8000
answer: Rule: every SONET/SDH frame lasts 125 µs, so 8000 frames per second. Rate = bytes per frame × 8 bits × 8000 = bytes per frame × 64 kb/s. One column of 9 bytes is worth 9 × 64 = 576 kb/s.
STM-1 = STS-3: 3 × 51.84 = 155.52 Mb/s, and 3 × 810 = 2430 bytes, so the STM-1 frame holds exactly the bytes of three byte-interleaved STS-1 frames.

E1s in one STM-1. Each E1 (2.048 Mb/s) is mapped into a VC-12 and then a TU-12 of 36 bytes per frame (36 × 64 kb/s = 2.304 Mb/s). Three TU-12s form a TUG-2, seven TUG-2s a TUG-3, and three TUG-3s fill the VC-4: 3 × 7 × 3 = 63 E1s.
Total E1 rate: 63 × 2.048 = 129.024 Mb/s. The TU-12s themselves occupy 63 × 2.304 = 145.152 Mb/s of the 149.76 Mb/s C-4; the other 8 columns are fixed stuff in the VC-4 and TUG-3 structure.
Efficiency: 129.024/155.52 = 0.830, so 83.0 percent of the STM-1 line rate is E1 user data. Dividing 155.52 by 2.048 would wrongly suggest 75 E1s.

What the overhead buys: the 5.184 Mb/s of section overhead carries framing, error checks between regenerators and multiplexers, the protection-switching bytes and the AU pointer; the path overhead checks the VC-4 end to end; and the TU-12 pointers let each E1 float with its own clock. That is why any one E1 can be added or dropped at an ADM without demultiplexing the other 62.
Closing check: 5.184 + 150.336 = 155.52 Mb/s and 0.576 + 149.76 = 150.336 Mb/s, so the parts add up to the whole at both levels.

bank.q: Design a fixed optical add-drop node for λ2 = 1550 nm using a fiber Bragg grating (n<sub>eff</sub> = 1.447) and two circulators. Each circulator pass costs 0.8 dB, the grating passes other channels with 0.3 dB loss and reflects λ2 with 0.2 dB loss and 30 dB rejection in transmission. Every channel arrives at −3 dBm. Find the grating pitch, the through and drop powers, the launch power for the added λ2, and the in-band crosstalk.
outline: Λ = λ<sub>B</sub>/(2n<sub>eff</sub>) = 535.6 nm
Signal routes through C1 and C2
Add: launch −3.1 dBm to match −4.9 dBm
Leaked old λ2: −34.6 dBm, 29.7 dB below the new λ2

answer.text: Grating pitch from the Bragg condition:

answer: Layout. The input line enters C1 port 1; C1 port 2 feeds the grating; the grating’s far end feeds C2 port 2; C2 port 3 is the output line. C1 port 3 is the drop port and C2 port 1 the add port. Draw the two circulators with the grating between them.
Routes. Through channels: C1 1→2, through the grating, C2 2→3. Dropped λ2: C1 1→2, reflected by the grating, C1 2→3. Added λ2: C2 1→2, reflected by the grating, C2 2→3.

answer.text: Power budget for each route (input −3 dBm per channel):

answer: Add launch power. To leave the node level with the through channels at −4.9 dBm, the added λ2 must be launched at −4.9 + 1.8 = −3.1 dBm.

answer.text: In-band crosstalk. The grating lets 30 dB of the incoming λ2 leak through, and this old λ2 reaches the output on the same wavelength as the new one:

answer: This crosstalk sits inside the new channel’s band, so no later filter can remove it; a grating with higher rejection (40 dB) would lower it to about −39.7 dB. Out-of-band crosstalk is set by the grating side lobes, so the grating should be apodized and its stop band kept narrower than the 0.8 nm spacing of a 100 GHz grid.
Why circulators: a 2×2 coupler in place of each circulator would cost at least 3 dB per pass (about 6 dB more on every route) and would let part of every channel into the drop port.
Closing check: through and add channels both leave at −4.9 dBm, and the drop receiver gets −4.8 dBm, about 1.8 to 1.9 dB below the input, as the losses add up to.

bank.q: Compare SOA and EDFA for a 10-channel WDM link in gain band, noise figure, polarization dependence, crosstalk, size and cost. Recommend one for a long-haul link of 10 spans and justify with numbers.
outline: EDFA: C-band 1530–1565 nm, gain 20–40 dB, NF 4–6 dB, small polarization dependence, slow (ms) gain dynamics so little inter-channel crosstalk, needs pump and metres of fiber
SOA: 1310 or 1550 nm, gain 20–30 dB, NF 6–9 dB, polarization dependent, sub-ns gain dynamics give cross-gain modulation, small and cheap
OSNR over 10 spans with NF 5 dB and 8 dB
Recommend EDFA for long haul; SOA for short links, gates and converters

head: Property
EDFA
SOA
rows: Er³⁺ ions in 10 to 30 m of silica fiber
current-driven semiconductor chip with anti-reflection facets
C-band 1530 to 1565 nm (L-band with longer fiber)
set by the material: near 1310 nm or 1550 nm
very small; the gain cannot follow the bits
pump laser, coupler, fiber coil; larger and dearer
one small chip, electrically pumped, cheap

answer: Crosstalk reasoning. In a 10-channel link each channel carries a changing bit pattern. In an SOA the gain recovers in under a nanosecond, so when one channel sends a 1 the gain seen by the other nine dips, and their bits pick up a copy of its pattern. In an EDFA the excited ions live about 10 ms, millions of bit periods at Gb/s rates, so the gain sees only the average power and the channels do not disturb each other.

Noise reasoning. NF depends on how complete the population inversion is. A 980 nm pumped EDFA reaches almost full inversion and has low coupling loss to the fiber; an SOA has partial inversion and loses power at the chip-to-fiber joints, so its NF is higher.

answer.text: Numbers for 10 spans (power into each amplifier −20 dBm per channel, OSNR in 0.1 nm):
answer.pre:
OSNR = 58 + P<sub>in</sub> − NF − 10 log₁₀ N,  10 log₁₀ 10 = 10 dB
EDFA, NF = 5 dB: OSNR = 58 − 20 − 5 − 10 = 23 dB
SOA,  NF = 8 dB: OSNR = 58 − 20 − 8 − 10 = 20 dB

answer: The SOA chain ends 3 dB worse before any cross-gain crosstalk is counted, and polarization changes along the fiber would make its gain wander by several dB from span to span.

Recommendation: EDFA for the 10-span long-haul link. It amplifies all 10 channels together in the C-band with low noise, negligible crosstalk and stable gain whatever the polarization; its higher cost is shared by all channels on every span.

Where the SOA wins: short metro and access links where cost and size matter more than noise, the 1310 nm band where erbium gives no gain, and switching uses (optical gates, wavelength converters by cross-gain modulation), where its fast gain is the point.
Closing check: going from 10 to 20 spans costs 10 log₁₀ 2 = 3.01 dB for either type, so the EDFA chain at 20 spans (20 dB) only matches the SOA chain at 10 spans.

bank.q: Explain how SPM and GVD interact in a fiber. Derive the condition for soliton formation and discuss the practical limits on soliton communication systems.
outline: GVD: in anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0) higher frequencies (blue) travel faster
SPM: red leading edge, blue trailing edge
Normal dispersion: chirps add, faster broadening; anomalous: they cancel
NLS equation and L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂|, L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀), N² = L<sub>D</sub>/L<sub>NL</sub>
N = 1: P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²), sech amplitude; higher orders breathe with z₀ = (π/2)L<sub>D</sub>
Limits: loss and amplifiers, ASE timing jitter, soliton interaction, high peak power; numbers
answer: GVD alone. Group-velocity dispersion β₂ makes different frequencies travel at different speeds. In anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0, the 1550 nm region of standard fiber) higher frequencies (blue) travel faster than lower ones (red); in normal dispersion (β₂ > 0) red is faster. Either way a pulse of width T₀ broadens over the dispersion length L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂|.

SPM alone. The Kerr effect gives φ<sub>NL</sub> = γP(T)L, and the frequency shift δω = −γL dP/dT puts red on the leading edge and blue on the trailing edge. The spectrum widens but the shape does not change by itself. The phase reaches 1 rad over the nonlinear length L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀).

head: Dispersion
Leading edge (red)
Trailing edge (blue)
Result
rows: chirps cancel; pulse can hold its shape

answer: Governing equation. The envelope A(z,T) obeys the nonlinear Schrödinger equation ∂A/∂z + (α/2)A + (iβ₂/2)∂²A/∂T² = iγ|A|²A. Ignoring loss and writing it with z in units of L<sub>D</sub> and the power in units of P₀ leaves one number, the soliton order N, with N² = L<sub>D</sub>/L<sub>NL</sub> = γP₀T₀²/|β₂|.

answer.text: Soliton condition. Balance needs equal lengths, N = 1:
answer.pre: L<sub>D</sub> = L<sub>NL</sub>  →  T₀²/|β₂| = 1/(γP₀)  →  P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²),  with β₂ < 0

answer: The exact solution is A(z,T) = √P₀ sech(T/T₀) e<sup>iz/(2L<sub>D</sub>)</sup>: the amplitude is sech-shaped (intensity sech²), the FWHM is 1.763 T₀, and only the phase grows with z. For N = 2, 3, … the pulse narrows, splits and recovers its shape after the soliton period z₀ = (π/2)L<sub>D</sub>.
Numbers. For β₂ = −20 ps²/km, γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹ and T₀ = 10 ps: L<sub>D</sub> = 100/20 = 5 km, P₀ = 20/(2 × 100) = 0.1 W, L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(2 × 0.1) = 5 km, so N = 1, and z₀ = 7.85 km.

Practical limits. (1) Loss: the fiber lowers the power, so SPM weakens between amplifiers and the balance holds only on average; amplifier spacing must be well below L<sub>D</sub>. (2) Amplifier noise: ASE shifts each soliton’s frequency at random, and dispersion turns this into timing jitter (the Gordon-Haus effect) that grows with distance. (3) Interaction: neighbouring solitons attract or repel, so the bit slot must be several pulse widths. (4) Power: 100 mW peaks per channel are high and bring other nonlinear crosstalk in WDM. These are why installed long-haul links use dispersion management and coherent detection instead.
Closing check: γP₀L<sub>D</sub> = 2 × 0.1 × 5 = 1 = N², and halving T₀ to 5 ps raises P₀ to 0.4 W, four times higher, which shows why short soliton pulses are costly in power.

bank.q: Explain the wavelength continuity constraint and blocking in WDM networks. Compare networks with no converters, sparse converters and full conversion at every node, using a worked path and the switch size of a node.
outline: Lightpath keeps one wavelength unless converted; S = S₁ ∩ … ∩ S<sub>k</sub>
Example A–B–C–D blocked with every link half free; converter at B fixes it
Blocking probability; RWA as graph colouring; first fit
Converter types: O-E-O, SOA cross-gain, four-wave mixing
Switch size W × F² against (FW)²; 128 against 1024
No, sparse and full conversion compared; recommendation
answer: Constraint. Without converters a lightpath must use the same wavelength on every link of its route. For links 1 to k with free sets S<sub>i</sub>, the request can be met only if S = S₁ ∩ S₂ ∩ … ∩ S<sub>k</sub> is not empty. Blocking is the event that S is empty (and no other route helps), and the blocking probability is the share of requests refused.

Intersection: {λ1, λ2} ∩ {λ2, λ3} = {λ2}; {λ2} ∩ {λ1, λ3} = ∅. The request is blocked although every link is only one-third busy. This is the cost of the constraint: free capacity exists but on the wrong wavelengths.
With a converter at B the path splits into A–B and B–C–D. A–B uses λ2; for B–C–D, {λ2, λ3} ∩ {λ1, λ3} = {λ3}. Convert λ2 → λ3 at B and the request is served with one conversion.

Converter types. O-E-O: detect, regenerate and retransmit on a new wavelength; mature, also cleans the signal, but tied to bit rate and format. SOA cross-gain modulation: the data on λ1 modulates the gain seen by a probe on λ2; all-optical but inverts and adds noise. Four-wave mixing: transparent to format but weak.

answer.text: Switch size for F = 4 fiber pairs, W = 8 wavelengths:
answer.pre:
no converters:   W planes of F × F  = 8 × 4² = 128 crosspoints
full conversion: (F W) × (F W)       = 32²     = 1024 crosspoints (+ up to 32 converters)

head: Design
Blocking
Cost and complexity
Wavelength assignment
rows: close to full conversion in many networks
moderate: converters only where paths meet
lowest: same as a circuit network with no wavelength rule
trivial: any free wavelength per link

answer: Analysis. Most blocking caused by the constraint comes from a few busy nodes where many long paths cross, so converters placed there remove most of it; adding them everywhere costs W times more crosspoints for little extra gain. Rerouting and reassigning existing lightpaths also lowers blocking without hardware.
Recommendation: sparse conversion at the high-degree, heavily loaded nodes, with first-fit assignment elsewhere; full conversion only where traffic is very dynamic and cost is secondary.
Closing check: 1024 ÷ 128 = 8 = W, the price of full conversion in this node, while one converter at B was enough to serve the blocked request.

bank.q: Explain the OSI seven-layer model, place SONET/SDH and ATM in it, and discuss why ATM used fixed 53-byte cells. Evaluate the cost of the cells for a 1500-byte IP packet.
outline: Seven layers and their PDUs
SONET/SDH mainly physical layer with framing; ATM layer 2 over it
ATM cell 5 + 48 bytes; header fields
Short fixed cells: low voice delay, simple fast switching, QoS classes
AAL5 on 1500 bytes: 32 cells, 1696 bytes, 88.4 %
Evaluation: lost to IP and Ethernet; ideas live on in MPLS

head: Layer
Job
PDU
rows: frames on one link, error check
bits on the medium: light, wavelength, power

answer: Placing SONET/SDH. SONET/SDH defines the optical interface, line rates and the framed byte structure with its overheads, so it sits at the physical layer, with framing and its own section, line and path layers inside it. The fiber and laser are its photonic layer.

Placing ATM. ATM switches cells between links using VPI/VCI labels, so it acts at layer 2 (some books place its virtual circuits partly at layer 3). The ATM adaptation layer cuts higher-layer data into cells. A typical stack is IP over AAL5 over ATM over SONET/SDH over fiber.
Cell format. 53 bytes: a 5-byte header (at the user interface 4-bit GFC, 8-bit VPI, 16-bit VCI, 3-bit payload type, 1-bit cell loss priority, 8-bit header error control) and a 48-byte payload.

Why short and fixed. (1) Voice delay: a 64 kb/s voice channel fills 48 bytes in 48 × 8 ÷ 64 000 = 6 ms; a longer cell would mean a longer fill delay and echo problems. (2) Switching: a fixed size lets hardware switch every cell in the same time with one table lookup, at line rate. (3) Queueing: a voice cell never waits behind a 1500-byte packet, so delay is bounded and the CBR and VBR-rt classes can be met.

answer.text: Cost for a 1500-byte IP packet over AAL5:

answer: Evaluation. Headers alone take 5/53 = 9.4 percent of every cell, and padding adds more for packets that do not fill the last cell: 11.6 percent of the link carries no user data here. IP was on every computer, Ethernet was cheap and kept getting faster, and carrying IP packets directly in Ethernet or on SONET/SDH and WDM avoided both the cell tax and ATM’s connection set-up. ATM lost the network core to IP, but its label switching and service classes live on in MPLS, and SONET/SDH and OTN still carry IP below.
Closing check: 1500 + 28 + 8 + 32 × 5 = 1696 bytes, the link total.

glossary.def: The drop in optical power caused by putting a component into the link, in dB.
The part of a coupler's loss not explained by the intended splitting ratio.
Leakage of one WDM channel into a neighbouring channel, measured in dB.
How little of the input power leaks back out of the other input-side port of a coupler, 10 log₁₀(P<sub>in</sub>/P₂) in dB.
A multi-port passive device that passes light in one rotational direction only, e.g. port 1 to 2 to 3.
Dielectric multilayer filter that passes one wavelength band and reflects the rest, used in add-drop modules.
A laser at 980 nm or 1480 nm whose power excites the erbium ions in an EDFA.
A state where more ions or carriers sit in the upper energy level than the lower one, so stimulated emission exceeds absorption.
Random photon emission that seeds amplifier noise and limits the noise figure.
The range of wavelengths over which an amplifier gives useful gain.
The output power at which amplifier gain falls 3 dB below its small-signal value.
Gain that differs for different input polarizations, a drawback of ordinary SOAs.
One channel's power changes the SOA gain seen by other channels, causing crosstalk.
L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂|, the distance over which group-velocity dispersion noticeably broadens a pulse of width parameter T₀.
L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀), the distance over which the SPM phase reaches 1 rad at peak power P₀.
The propagation equation combining GVD and SPM that governs pulse shape in a fiber.
A change of instantaneous frequency across a pulse, so different parts of the pulse have different wavelengths.
The regime where β₂ < 0 and higher frequencies (shorter wavelengths) travel faster; required for bright solitons.
A device that shifts a lightpath from one wavelength to another, removing the continuity constraint.
A node that switches wavelengths from any input fiber to any output fiber.
The chance that a requested lightpath cannot be set up because no wavelength is free.
Packing tributary channels into fixed positions of a frame locked to one master clock.
Nearly but not exactly synchronous, so bit stuffing is needed before multiplexing, as in the PDH hierarchy.
SONET/SDH overhead bytes used for framing, error checking and management at each level.
One level of a layered model that performs a defined job and uses the services of the level below.
A connection whose route is fixed at setup time and identified by a short label in each cell.
The share of a coupler’s total output that leaves one chosen port, in percent.
The signal power an amplifier adds divided by the pump power it uses.
The 87-column part of a SONET frame that carries the path overhead and the user payload.
The ATM adaptation layer for data: pads the packet and adds an 8-byte trailer so it fills whole 48-byte payloads.
